To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pathogenicity associated with co-challenge with vvIBDV and endemic IBDV was dependent on age of inoculation and pathogenicity of the IBDV strain.
the pathogenicity of vvIBDV can be reduced by simultaneous infection with other IBDV strains.
co-infection with vvIBDV and IBDV strains endemic in the US results in a significant decrease of the severity of disease in chickens challenged at 4 weeks but not 6 weeks of old.

the pathogenicity of co-challenge of chickens with a very virulent strain of Infectious Bursal Disease Virus (IBDV) and the IBDV strains endemic in the U.S.
the pathogenicity induced in chickens by simultaneous challenge with vvIBDV and IBDV endemic in the United states.

coinfection with vvIBDV and the endemic strains of IBDV resulted in a decrease in mortality and severity in bursa lesions, and that this decrease in disease was dependent on the pathotype of IBDV co-inoculated.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
co-challenge with rIBDV and IBDV strains endemic in the U.S. resulted in significant reductions in mortality and severity (lesion score) of disease in 4-week-old birds.
the pathogenicity of vvIBDV is reduced in chickens co-infected with less pathogenic strains of IBDV.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the pathogenicity of vvIBDV can be significantly reduced in co-challenge experiments.
co-challenge with rIBDV and IBDV strains endemic in the US can result in a significant reduction in disease severity.
co-infection with vvIBDV and IBDV strains endemic in the US can result in a significant reduction in severity of disease.
